           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                    )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                      )
         FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                         )
         APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA LARGE LOAD                     )
         TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                     )   CASE NO. PUD2026-000046
         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                           )
         CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                    )
         RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                          )
         PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                        )




                                            Rebuttal Testimony

                                                    of

                                           Matthew DeCourcey

                                               on behalf of

                                    Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company




                                              October 5, 2026
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 72 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 31




    1                              I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY
    2    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    3    A.    My name is Matthew DeCourcey. My business address is 200 Clarendon Street, Boston,
    4          Massachusetts 02116.
    5
    6    Q.    Are you the same Matthew DeCourcey who filed Direct Testimony in this case on
    7          June 17, 2026?
    8    A.    Yes.
    9
   10    Q.    What is the purpose of your Rebuttal Testimony?
   11    A.    My Rebuttal Testimony responds to intervenor testimony on the subjects I addressed in my
   12          Direct Testimony: how the Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) Tariff compares to
   13          large load tariffs approved in other jurisdictions, how its provisions protect OG&E’s other
   14          customers from stranded costs and cross-subsidies, and whether adding XLPL customers
   15          could put downward pressure on rates.
   16                 Specifically, I address (1) how the Commission should use the tariff surveys and
   17          peer comparisons on which several intervenors rely; (2) recommendations to limit the
   18          tariff’s applicability by end use rather than size; (3) recommendations to shorten the
   19          minimum term, change the basis of the termination and capacity reduction fees, and reduce
   20          the collateral and billing minimum requirements; (4) the class rate design determinants and
   21          the Customer Class Protection Charge (“CCPC”); (5) Attorney General witness Lewis’s
   22          critique of the rate benefit analysis I referenced in my Direct Testimony; and (6) the various
   23          “Delivery Only Deregulated Generation Election” (“DODGE”) proposals.
   24
   25    Q.    How does your Rebuttal Testimony relate to that of other OG&E witnesses?
   26    A.    OG&E witness Gwin Cash addresses tariff design issues, including the treatment of
   27          incremental load and metering, the Minimum Billing Energy provision, the class rate
   28          design determinants, the CCPC methodology, the timing of allocation factor updates, clean
   29          energy options, and the Customer Affordability and Reservation Charges. OG&E witness
   30          John Laws addresses the Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) requirement, the
   31          contract term and renewal provisions, the termination and capacity reduction fees,
         Rebuttal Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey
         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                             Page 1 of 29
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 72 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 31




    1          collateral, the Preliminary Agreement, and late payment provisions. OG&E witness Adam
    2          Snapp addresses the power factor requirement, grid-enhancing technologies, and customer
    3          self-build of interconnection facilities. OG&E witness Kimber Shoop addresses the
    4          applicability of the XLPL Tariff, proposals for Commission review of individual
    5          agreements and related resource-adequacy and load-ramp protections; proposals that
    6          would permit XLPL customers to obtain generation outside OG&E’s bundled service
    7          framework, referred to here as DODGE proposals; and the requested regulatory asset for
    8          portfolio optimization software. OG&E witness Kelly Riley discusses commentary offered
    9          in intervenor testimony regarding interruptible service and demand-side management
   10          programs for XLPL customers, and resource adequacy concerns regarding DODGE
   11          proposals. Where my testimony touches on some of those subjects, the purpose is to
   12          describe industry standards and practice and to comment on relevant evidence from other
   13          settings and jurisdictions, I rely on testimony from OG&E employees for the Company’s
   14          positions.
   15
   16    Q.    Please summarize your conclusions.
   17    A.    First, the intervenors’ own surveys largely confirm what I concluded in my Direct
   18          Testimony: the core terms of the XLPL Tariff fall within the range of large load tariffs
   19          approved elsewhere, and in several respects provide more protection than is typical. Where
   20          intervenors recommend changes, they generally propose moving individual provisions to
   21          the median or average of a survey. A median is a descriptive statistic, not a standard of
   22          reasonableness, and selecting the median of each provision separately would produce a
   23          combination of terms that no commission has approved and whose overall level of
   24          protection no party has evaluated.
   25                  Second, defining applicability by the size of the service obligation a customer
   26          creates, rather than by its end use, is consistent with the prevailing practice reflected in the
   27          intervenors’ own surveys and with the principle—advanced by Google’s own witness—
   28          that customers should be classified by their electrical characteristics rather than by their
   29          industry.
   30                  Third, the minimum term, termination and capacity reduction fees, collateral,
   31          billing minimums work and other customer commercial terms and customer protections
         Rebuttal Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey
         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                               Page 2 of 29
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 72 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 31




    1          that are specified in the XLPL Tariff are intended to work as complimentary components
    2          of an integrated package. The recommended modifications would each weaken that
    3          package without a corresponding showing that the remaining provisions would be
    4          strengthened to compensate. I also clarify how the three-year limit on the termination fee
    5          operates, which confirms that an XLPL customer pays at least its Minimum Charges for
    6          the full Initial Term.
    7                  Fourth, the use of Maximum Contract Demand for cost allocation and minimum
    8          billing determinants for rate design serve distinct and complementary purposes, and the
    9          CCPC provides a protection that, according to the intervenors’ own survey, none of the
   10          surveyed tariffs contains.
   11                  Fifth, the cost-of-service analysis that the Company developed in order to
   12          understand the impacts on existing customers from a data center customer, results of which
   13          were presented to the Commission in Case No. PUD 2026-000031 is methodologically
   14          appropriate and yields reasonable results. Observations that the analysis excludes the cost
   15          of serving the new data are factually accurate, but assertions that follow which suggest that
   16          the framework ignores important cost information are incorrect. The ratemaking the
   17          Company is proposing accounts for all the relevant costs that could be incurred to serve
   18          new data center customers and the XLPL Tariff includes provisions that will mitigate the
   19          risk from unintended effectives. A demonstration that the Tariff effectively protects the
   20          Company’s customers from adverse impacts provides sufficient support for its approval
   21          unto itself. That the protections included in the XLPL Tariff will effectively mitigate
   22          customers’ exposure to risk has been well established in this proceeding.
   23                  Finally, I explain my primary arguments against the DODGE proposals and how
   24          those proposals could increase risks for existing customers.
   25                  I continue to recommend that the Commission approve the core protections of the
   26          XLPL Tariff and the Terms and Conditions of Service for Extra Large Load Customers
   27          (“T&CXLLC”) as filed, together with the limited clarifications that OG&E witnesses Cash
   28          and Laws describe in their Rebuttal Testimony.




         Rebuttal Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey
         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                            Page 3 of 29

    1                           II. THE USE OF PEER TARIFF COMPARISONS
    2    Q.      Several intervenors present surveys or comparisons of large load tariffs. What do
    3            they show?
    4    A.      For the most part, they confirm the conclusions in my Direct Testimony.                     Several
    5            intervenors reported the parameters of approved large load rate designs. Their findings
    6            show that parameters vary between instances and that OG&E’s proposed design is
    7            consistent with large load tariffs in use at other utilities.
    8
    9    Q.      Can you provide some examples?
   10    A.      The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”) witness Dismukes surveyed thirteen
   11            approved large load rate designs. He finds that the XLPL Tariff’s 75 MW threshold equals
   12            the median of the surveyed tariffs, that the 85 percent minimum billing demand is above
   13            the median but “still within a normal range,” that the 15-year minimum term and five-year
   14            maximum load ramp are consistent with his survey, that an exit fee equal to the remaining
   15            minimum charges is consistent with tariffs approved in other jurisdictions, and that the
   16            CIAC requirement is similar in nature to other tariffs that include one.1
   17                    Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”) witness Dauphinais likewise
   18            acknowledges that OG&E’s proposed minimum billing demand is within “the range of
   19            what has been selected by utilities elsewhere.”2
   20                    Google witness Kimbrough describes an exit fee based on remaining contractual
   21            minimum charges as “a reasonable, practical, and well-established regulatory approach,”
   22            and cites several tariffs he reviewed that include them. Regarding contract term, Mr.
   23            Kimbrough concludes that “[a] 15-year contract term can be reasonable for a customer
   24            taking full-service requirements capacity and energy supply from OG&E.”3

    2    A.    Yes, quite a few changes have been offered. Many are proposals to adjust the customer

   20          lowering the minimum billing demand and reducing the collateral requirement to the
   21          median values from the tariffs he reviewed (80% and 24 months, respectively). Mr.
   22          Kimbrough contends that his preferred value for minimum billing demand is the
   23          “prevailing industry average.”         Mr. Dauphinais bases his recommendation to lower the

    1          minimum contract term to 10 years on his conclusion that more than half of the tariffs in
    2          my comparison have minimum terms of 8 to 12 years.
    3
    4    Q.    Considered     themselves,     would       the   Commission’s     acceptance      of   these
    5          recommendations increase or decrease risks to OG&E’s customers?
    6    A.    All else equal, each of these recommendations would increase customers’ risk.
    7
    8    Q.    Is a survey median an appropriate method for setting individual tariff provisions?
    9    A.    No. Statistical measures like medians and averages can provide useful insights but are not
   10          an appropriate basis for regulation. Many of the recommendations made by intervenors
   11          could be fairly characterized as “different but not better.” The evidence presented does not
   12          show that a tariff parameter that falls above the median of a reported range is unreasonable
   13          or that customers’ interest would be better promoted by setting a tariff parameter on the
   14          basis of a calculated median or average.
   15
   16    Q.    Do you have any other concerns about the idea of adjusting tariff terms in this
   17          manner?
   18    A.    Yes. The customer protection provisions of a large load tariff must be considered as a
   19          whole. Commissions and parties trade provisions off against one another and against the
   20          circumstances of the particular utility—its resource position, the size and pace of its large
   21          load pipeline, the rules of its regional transmission organization, and any statutory
   22          directives that apply. A tariff with a shorter term may compensate with a larger exit fee or
   23          more collateral; a tariff with a lower minimum bill may require a longer commitment.
   24          Setting terms based on survey data ignores the broader perspective and increases the
   25          potential for unintended consequences.
   26
   27    Q.    Can you illustrate that point using the record in this case?
   28    A.    Yes. Table R-1 compares the XLPL Tariff to two large load designs that intervenors
   29          themselves placed in the record—the Indiana Michigan Power Company (“I&M”)
   30          Michigan large load provisions that Mr. Dauphinais attached as Exhibit JRD-4, and the

    2          PSO settlement tariff, which is Dr. Dismukes’s principal Oklahoma reference point,
    3          requires 48 months of collateral—twice the 24-month median he recommends here.8
    4                  I am not suggesting that the Commission adopt either of those tariffs. The point is
    5          that reasonableness is evaluated on the package as a whole, and every approved design in
    6          the record departs from the median somewhere. The XLPL Tariff should be evaluated the
    7          same way.
    8
    9    Q.    Should the PSO settlement tariff be treated as the benchmark for the XLPL Tariff?
   10    A.    It should be considered with caution, for the reasons OG&E witness Laws explains. The
   11          stipulation was contested, PSO and the Attorney General did not join it, and the
   12          Commission has not yet acted on the Administrative Law Judge’s recommendation.9 Its
   13          terms also reflect negotiated trade-offs among the settling parties that do not carry over to
   14          a different utility on a different record. To the extent the PSO settlement is relevant, it
   15          confirms that Oklahoma stakeholders—including large load customers—accepted a 15-
   16          year commitment, substantial collateral, and a mechanism to address system cost impacts
   17          on other customers. Each of those features is also present in the XLPL Tariff.
   18
   19                           III. APPLICABILITY BASED ON LOAD SIZE
   20    Q.    OIEC witness Dauphinais and Walmart witness Marchand recommend limiting the
   21          XLPL Tariff to new data centers, cryptocurrency mining operations, and artificial-
   22          intelligence computing facilities, consistent with the definition of “large load
   23          customer” in HB 2992. How do you respond?
   24    A.    I am not an attorney, and I do not offer an opinion on what HB 2992 requires or permits.
   25          Those questions will be addressed by counsel. I address the related ratemaking question:
   26          whether it is reasonable, as a matter of tariff design and industry practice, to apply large

    1          load protections based on the size of the service obligation a customer creates rather than
    2          on the customer’s end use. In my opinion, it is.
    3
    4    Q.    How do other jurisdictions define the applicability of large load tariffs?
    5    A.    Most define applicability by load size.       As Dr. Dismukes observes, “[w]hile some
    6          jurisdictions have created tariffs explicitly limited to data center customers, most have
    7          defined applicability of tariffs based on a minimum load size, irrespective of
    8          industrial/economic sector of the end use.”10 Of the thirteen tariffs in his Exhibit DED-1,
    9          only Ohio Power Company’s Data Center Tariff limits applicability by end use.11 The
   10          I&M Michigan provisions that Mr. Dauphinais attached apply to customers whose contract
   11          capacity is, or is reasonably expected to grow to, 50 MW or more, without regard to end
   12          use.12
   13
   14    Q.    Why is load size an appropriate basis for applicability from a ratemaking
   15          perspective?
   16    A.    When a customer asks OG&E to plan for 75 MW or more of new load, OG&E must plan
   17          and procure accredited capacity and build the infrastructure needed to serve that load on
   18          the customer’s schedule. The two risks I identified in my Direct Testimony—that those
   19          commitments outlast the customer’s load (stranded cost) and that the resulting costs are
   20          spread to other classes (cross-subsidy)—arise from the scale and timing of the
   21          commitment. A 100 MW industrial expansion and a 100 MW data center require the same
   22          amount of accredited capacity.
   23                   Google witness Kimbrough makes a closely related point. He testifies that a utility
   24          should not “single out” customers that impose equivalent cost profiles based on non-
   25          electrical characteristics “such as their business model, industry sector, or end-use,” and
   26          that customers should instead be classified on physical electrical characteristics such as

    1          interconnection voltage, peak demand and load profile, and load factor and power factor.13
    2          The XLPL applicability criteria do exactly that.


    3    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais argues that computational loads present an elevated stranded cost
    4          risk that traditional commercial and industrial loads do not. Do you agree?
    5    A.    Not necessarily.     I agree that computational loads have characteristics that warrant
    6          particular attention, which explains the proliferation of new tariffs and regulations across
    7          the industry. But Mr. Dauphinais’ characterization is too broad. Service for other kinds
    8          of large customers can also require significant utility investments and some commercial
    9          and industrial customers create significant counterparty risk. Mr. Dauphinais himself
   10          describes industrial demand as, in most cases, “cyclical and tied to production schedules,
   11          maintenance outages and market conditions.”14 Industrial facilities do curtail or close in
   12          response to market conditions, and when a facility of 75 MW or more does so after OG&E
   13          has procured resources to serve it, the effect on other customers is the same regardless of
   14          the facility’s industry.
   15                  Notwithstanding any of the above, the potential for adverse impacts to customers
   16          arises from unhedged stranded cost risk. As I describe at length in my Direct Testimony,
   17          the customer protections against stranded cost risk that OG&E is proposing are robust.
   18
   19    Q.    Are there practical considerations that favor a size-based test?
   20    A.    Yes.    A size threshold is objective and measurable.        An end-use test requires a
   21          determination of a facility’s “primary function,” which may be difficult for facilities that
   22          combine computing with other operations and invites disputes over classification. I also
   23          note that Walmart’s stated concern is that its distribution and fulfillment facilities “can
   24          approach or exceed 50 MW over a planning horizon,” and Walmart supports the 75 MW
   25          threshold as a “regulatory buffer” that prevents such facilities from being swept into the

    3                                 IV. STRANDED COST PROTECTIONS
    4          A. Minimum Term
    5    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais recommends reducing the minimum term from 15 years to 10 years,
    6          noting that more than half of the tariffs in your comparison have terms of 8 to 12
    7          years. How do you respond?
    8    A.    His count is accurate; six of the eleven comparison tariffs in Table 1 of my Direct
    9          Testimony have minimum terms in that range.16                    But it does not support his
   10          recommendation, for three reasons.
   11                     First, as I explained above, a minimum term cannot be evaluated in isolation from
   12          the other provisions with which it was paired. Second, the minimum terms in Table 1 are
   13          not measured on a uniform basis; as I noted in my Direct Testimony, most begin after a
   14          ramp period, but some do not.17 Third, the record contains a number of approved or
   15          recommended designs with minimum terms of 15 years or longer: Consumers Energy and
   16          Santee Cooper (15 years), Virginia Electric and Power Company (14 years), Florida Power
   17          & Light and Kentucky Power (20 years), the I&M Michigan provisions (at least 15 years
   18          following a ramp of up to five years), and the PSO settlement tariff (15 years). 18 Dr.
   19          Dismukes found the 15-year term consistent with his survey and recommends no change,
   20          and Mr. Kimbrough accepts a 15-year term for full-requirements customers.19 HB 2992’s
   21          requirement that the term be “at least ten (10) years” establishes a floor, not a target.

    1    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais contends that a 10-year term would be just as protective if the
    2          termination fee were based on the remaining net plant of incremental investments less
    3          their residual value to other customers. Do you agree?
    4    A.    No. In practice, that calculation requires the Commission to identify which production
    5          resources were acquired to serve a particular customer and to estimate the residual value
    6          of those resources to other customers at some future date. Attorney General witness Beling
    7          explains why the first of those determinations is “very difficult,” given that resource needs
    8          are driven by several factors and commercial operation dates rarely coincide with a new
    9          load’s start date.20     The second depends on assumptions about future load, market
   10          conditions, and accreditation that will themselves be contested.
   11                  Neither value can be known when the customer signs its agreement, so neither party
   12          can quantify the obligation in advance, and the collateral requirement could not be sized
   13          against it. Mr. Dauphinais’s proposal would therefore trade a known contractual obligation
   14          for a contested estimate resolved after the customer has left, and it would shorten the
   15          term—the most certain of the protections—in reliance on the least certain. OG&E witness
   16          Laws addresses this recommendation further.
   17
   18    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais also recommends that a fee apply when a customer departs at the
   19          end of its initial term. How do you respond?
   20    A.    OG&E witness Laws addresses this recommendation. I am not aware of any tariff currently
   21          in effect that includes a fee like the one Mr. Dauphinais describes. It is not an element of
   22          any of the tariffs described in Table 1 of my Direct Testimony or in Dr. Dismukes’s Exhibit

    2    Q.    PUD witness Scalf states that describing the XLPL exit fee as “remaining contract

    5    A.    I appreciate Mr. Scalf’s careful review of the comparison, and his observation warrants a
    6          clarification of how the three-year limit operates.21 Under Section 2.03 of the Electric
    7          Service Agreement (“ESA”), a customer may not give notice of an Elective Termination
    8          until it has completed the ninth Contract Year of the Initial Term, and the notice period
    9          must be at least 36 months.22 The earliest an Elective Termination can take effect is
   10          therefore after the twelfth Contract Year, at which point no more than three years of the
   11          15-year Initial Term remain. The three-year limit coincides with the maximum remaining
   12          term; it does not reduce the fee below the Minimum Charges that remain. (The one-year
   13          floor, by contrast, can require a fee greater than the remaining Minimum Charges if the
   14          termination takes effect late in the term.)
   15                  During the notice period, an XLPL customer would continue to take service and
   16          pay at least its monthly Minimum Charges. As OG&E witness Shoop explained in Direct
   17          Testimony, the effect is that the fee will not exceed three years of Minimum Charges
   18          precisely because the customer cannot give notice before year nine.23 The customer
   19          therefore pays at least its Minimum Charges for the entire Initial Term, as I stated in my
   20          Direct Testimony.24 The Capacity Reduction Fee is structured the same way.25 And if the
   21          agreement is terminated for a Triggering Event, Section 2.04(c) of the ESA makes the
   22          customer responsible for the Minimum Charges for the remaining duration of the Term,
   23          without a three-year limit.26 In my view, “remaining contract minimums” accurately
   24          describes the XLPL exit fee.

   25                 For example, OG&E must still maintain resource adequacy, transmission

   27          and contingency capabilities necessary to serve the customer’s load when its contracted

    4    Q.    Does DODGE create any long-term supply risks?
    5    A.    Yes. OG&E’s planning framework is designed around long-lived utility infrastructure
    6          intended to serve long-term contractual obligations. DODGE proposals often contemplate
    7          arrangements involving separately negotiated power purchase agreements or capacity
    8          supply arrangements that may have substantially shorter lives than the utility service

   11          customer’s load remains connected to and dependent upon the utility system. In that
   12          circumstance, OG&E and its remaining customers could face significant pressure to
   13          procure substitute resources in future market conditions that may be substantially different
   14          and potentially more expensive than current conditions. That is an exposure that does not
   15          exist to the same degree under the utility-owned or utility-procured model.

   17    Q.    Are there operational considerations associated with DODGE that should concern the
   18          Commission?
   19    A.    Yes. The electric system functions as an integrated portfolio rather than a collection of
   20          isolated resources. Utility-owned and utility-managed resources can be economically
   21          dispatched, cycled, maintained, optimized, or temporarily replaced by other resources
   22          depending upon system conditions.
   23                  Under a DODGE framework, it is less clear how privately supplied resources would
   24          interact with normal utility portfolio optimization and dispatch practices. Questions arise
   25          concerning outage coordination, maintenance planning, economic dispatch, reliability
   26          obligations, fuel and market optimization, and how the costs of those activities would be
   27          allocated among customers. These complexities are not merely administrative. Utility
   28          resource portfolios are planned, dispatched, maintained, optimized, and replaced as
   29          integrated systems. The economic value of a utility-owned generation fleet is not limited
   30          to the output of any single generating unit. Utilities continuously optimize generation
   31          dispatch, maintenance schedules, outage management, fuel procurement, reserve

    8    A.    No.    Renewable energy opportunities can be pursued through customer-specific
    9          arrangements without requiring the Commission to adopt a DODGE framework. As
   10          discussed by other Company witnesses, OG&E has demonstrated a willingness to evaluate

   15    Q.    What conclusion do you draw regarding DODGE proposals?
   16    A.    In my opinion, proponents of DODGE frequently emphasize potential benefits while
   17          giving insufficient weight to the additional risks such proposals create. The record does
   18          not demonstrate that DODGE would reduce costs, accelerate resource development, or
   19          lower risk to existing customers. Conversely, there are numerous ways in which DODGE
   20          could increase risk. These include greater counterparty risk, increased competition for
   21          generation resources and interconnection opportunities, reduced contributions toward
   22          embedded generation costs, additional operational complexity, less integrated resource
   23          planning, reduced regulatory oversight of generation procurement decisions, and continued
   24          reliance on utility reliability services even where utility generation charges are reduced or
   25          eliminated.
   26                 In my opinion, the XLPL tariff achieves an appropriate balance by allowing large-
   27          load customers to participate in the benefits of Oklahoma’s integrated utility system while
   28          ensuring those customers continue contributing toward the costs and obligations necessary
   29          to operate that system reliably. DODGE proposals materially weaken that balance and
   30          shift the framework away from the integrated utility model that underlies the customer
   31          protections contained throughout the XLPL tariff.

    2    Q.    Please summarize your Rebuttal Testimony.
    3    A.    The intervenors’ own evidence confirms that the core provisions of the XLPL Tariff fall
    4          within the range of approved large load tariffs and, in several respects, provide more
    5          protection than is typical. Survey medians are not a standard of reasonableness, and
    6          adopting the median of each provision separately would produce an untested combination
    7          of terms that corresponds to no approved tariff. Size-based applicability is consistent with
    8          prevailing practice and with the principle that customers are classified by their electrical
    9          characteristics. The minimum term, termination and capacity reduction fees, collateral,
   10          and billing minimums operate as an integrated package, and the exit fee does recover the
   11          remaining Minimum Charges for the Initial Term. The rate design determinants and the
   12          CCPC protect other classes, and the CCPC methodology should be established when actual
   13          data are available, as Mr. Cash recommends. Mr. Lewis is correct that the shared-cost
   14          analysis isolates one effect, but the tariff’s design, especially the CCPC, addresses the
   15          necessary protections. Finally, I believe the Commission should reject the DODGE
   16          proposals. I agree with the conclusions contained in the Rebuttal Testimony of OG&E
   17          witness Shoop and have explained why I believe DODGE proposals create more risk for
   18          existing customers.
   19                 I recommend that the Commission approve the core protections of the XLPL Tariff
